newsitem.title: UK: All metal prices bar copper seen rising next year.
newsitem.headline: All metal prices bar copper seen rising next year.

text.p: Prices for all base metals trading on the London Metal Exchange (LME) are forecast to rise in 1997 except copper, which is expected to be sharply lower, analysts at the LME metals seminar said on Monday.
Most markets had performed considerably worse than analysts had predicted at the start of 1996, with copper's mid-year crash doing little to lift the gloom.

But against a background of falling stocks, rising demand and the likely re-emergence of fund investment buying next year, the other five metals were seen de-coupling from the red metal and heading higher, the analysts said.
--ALUMINIUM - LME prices were likely to rise to $1,680 a tonne in 1997, up 10 percent from $1,524 in 1996, said Kevin Crisp of U.S. investment house J.P Morgan.
"We think the tide for aluminium is already turning," he said. Current weakness which has pushed the market to fresh 2-1/2 year lows on Monday was merely "fog on the road," he said.
Crisp said consumption growth should pick up in 1997 after being flat in 1996, while Russian exports to the West would fall. Firmer values in 1997 would provide the base for sharper rallies in 1998.
--COPPER - Cash copper prices were heading for a 1997 average of $1,896, down sharply from the $2,332 average so far this year, said Malcolm Southwood of J.B. Were and Son Ltd.
He forecast a supply surplus of 300,000 tonnes next year.

Southwood said a number of factors would prevent a sustained price recovery, including hedge selling associated with unwinding of copper positions, LME warrants being more readily available to the market and smelter capacity rising.
--LEAD - Prices were heading for slightly higher levels of 39 cents a pound ($860/tonne) in 1997 from 37 cents ($816) in 1996, Claire Hassal of Brook Hunt and Associates said.
The Western world supply deficit was due to move closer into balance next year, with the shortfall in 1996 of 90,000 tonnes likely to shrink to a deficit of 17,000 tonnes in 1997.
--NICKEL - The market was set to rebound to $8,598 in 1997 from $7,826 in 1996, with a further rally to $9,370 in 1998, said Robin Bhar, analyst at LME brokers Brandeis.
He forecast demand to rise by four percent in 1997 on the back of a modest bounce in stainless steel production.
Russian exports of the metal to the West are expected to be around 156,000 tonnes this year, in line with the previous year's levels, Bhar said.
--TIN - The tin market was in for a strong rebound in 1997, with supplies likely to lag demand in the Western world by nearly 10,000 tonnes, William Adams of broker Rudolf Wolff said.
He pegged three month prices to average at $6,800 next year from a 1996 average around $6,280.

--ZINC - Stocks are likely to fall towards critically low levels by the end of 1997, boosting values to $1,320 by late-1997 from current prices just above $1,000, said Tariq Salaria of Metal Bulletin Research (MBR).
As well as falling inventories, investment fund buying and the possibility of tight control of world stocks could fuel the rally, he said.
